learningObjectives: Apply Newton's second law to inclined plane problems
Resolve weight into components parallel and perpendicular to incline

prompt.text:
A child sits on a smooth plastic slide at a playground. The slide makes an angle of 40° with the ground. If the child has a mass of 25 kg and friction is negligible, calculate:

(a) The acceleration of the child as they slide down
(b) The force the slide exerts perpendicular to its surface

Use g = 10 m/s²
prompt.context: Assume the child can be modeled as a point mass. The slide surface is perfectly smooth.

assets.alt: Child on an inclined slide at 40 degrees

steps.prompt: What type of physics problem is this?

explanations.micro: This is an inclined plane problem - object moving along a sloped surface.
explanations.conceptual: When an object moves along a tilted surface under gravity, we use inclined plane analysis.
explanations.hint: Look at the geometry - the child moves along a slope.

mistakeMapping.message: Projectile motion involves objects moving through air in a parabolic path.
Circular motion requires the object to move in a circle.

steps.prompt: Draw the free body diagram for the child. What forces act on them?

explanations.micro: Two forces: Weight (mg) downward, Normal force (N) perpendicular to slide.
explanations.conceptual: For any object on a surface, identify gravity and the contact force from the surface.
explanations.deep: The normal force is always perpendicular to the contact surface, not vertical. This is a common source of confusion.
explanations.hint: What pulls the child down? What prevents them from falling through the slide?

mistakeMapping.message: The problem states friction is negligible - don't include friction force.

steps.prompt: What is the component of weight parallel to the slide (down the incline)?

explanations.micro: Weight component along incline = mg sin(θ)
explanations.conceptual: The angle θ is between the incline and horizontal. The component along the incline uses sine.
explanations.deep: Draw the weight vector and project it onto the incline direction. The angle between weight and the perpendicular to incline equals θ.
explanations.contrast: sin gives the component along the incline, cos gives the component perpendicular to it. A common mistake is swapping these.
explanations.hint: Which trig function relates the opposite side to the hypotenuse?

mistakeMapping.message: You've swapped sin and cos. Draw the triangle carefully - sin is for the component along the incline.

steps.prompt: Calculate the acceleration of the child down the slide. Enter your answer in m/s².

explanations.conceptual: Apply F = ma along the incline. The only force along the incline is mg sin(θ), so ma = mg sin(θ), giving a = g sin(θ).
explanations.deep: Notice that mass cancels out - all objects slide down a frictionless incline with the same acceleration regardless of mass!
explanations.hint: What is the net force along the incline? Apply Newton's second law.

mistakeMapping.message: You used cos instead of sin. The component along the incline uses sin(θ).
You used g directly without resolving into components. The acceleration along the incline is g sin(θ), not g.

steps.prompt: Calculate the normal force exerted by the slide on the child. Enter your answer in N.

explanations.conceptual: Perpendicular to the incline, forces must balance (no acceleration in that direction). So N = mg cos(θ).
explanations.deep: The normal force is less than the weight (191.5 N vs 250 N) because only the perpendicular component of weight is supported by the surface.
explanations.hint: What is the component of weight perpendicular to the slide? The normal force balances this.

mistakeMapping.message: You used sin instead of cos. The normal force balances the perpendicular component: mg cos(θ).
You used mg directly. On an incline, N ≠ mg. The normal force equals mg cos(θ).

steps.prompt: Sanity check: If the angle were 0° (flat ground), what would be the acceleration and normal force?

explanations.micro: At θ = 0°: a = g sin(0°) = 0, N = mg cos(0°) = mg. Object at rest on flat ground.
explanations.conceptual: Limiting cases help verify your formula. At θ = 0°, the 'incline' is flat, so no acceleration and full weight supported.
explanations.deep: Always check limiting cases: θ = 0° (flat) and θ = 90° (vertical drop). Your formulas should give physically sensible results.

synthesis: This is an inclined plane problem with a single body and no friction.
Forces: Weight (mg = 250 N) downward, Normal force perpendicular to surface.
Resolve weight: mg sin(40°) = 160.7 N along incline, mg cos(40°) = 191.5 N perpendicular.
Apply F = ma along incline: a = g sin(40°) = 6.43 m/s².
Equilibrium perpendicular: N = mg cos(40°) = 191.5 N.

limitingCases.why: On flat ground, object doesn't accelerate and full weight is supported.
Free fall - no contact with surface.

alternativePaths.label: Energy method
outline: Use conservation of energy: mgh = ½mv²
h = L sin(θ) where L is slide length
Find v at bottom, then use kinematics to get a

solutions.fullDerivation:
Along incline: $\sum F_{\parallel} = ma$
$mg\sin\theta = ma$
$a = g\sin\theta = 10 \times \sin(40°) = 6.43$ m/s²

Perpendicular to incline: $\sum F_{\perp} = 0$
$N - mg\cos\theta = 0$
$N = mg\cos\theta = 25 \times 10 \times \cos(40°) = 191.5$ N

authoring.notes: Generated from HC-Verma inclined plane pattern. Good introductory problem.
